Duane’s syndrome, November 2025

# **Duane’s syndrome**
**This leaflet explains the eye condition known as Duane’s syndrome, how the condition effects eye movement and what management options are available, if required.**

## **What is Duane’s syndrome?**
Duane’s syndrome is a horizontal eye movement difference, which is present from birth but is often not noticed until the child is older. Duane’s syndrome can affect either eye or both eyes.

## **What causes Duane’s syndrome?**
In Duane’s syndrome there is mis-wiring of the nerves to the eye muscles. This means the eye muscles do not receive the correct signals, making it harder for the eyes to move in certain directions – in this case, side to side.

## **Other features of Duane’s syndrome include:**
• Changes to the eyelids when looking side to side. • People with Duane’s often move their head to look to the side rather than just use their eyes alone.
• Head posture change, where the head can be seen to turn towards the affected side.
• Strabismus (turn in the eye or squint) and a need for glasses.

## **What is the treatment for Duane’s syndrome?**
### Children with Duane’s syndrome are regularly monitored up until the age of 7 but generally, they do not need treatment. Children often have a slight change to their head posture to compensate for their eye muscle restriction which typically remains present into adulthood.

## **Advice for parents and carers**
• If your child has a change to their head posture, **do not** correct this, as correction can cause visual symptoms such as double vision and difficulty for your child to use their eyes together as a pair, causing visual discomfort.

# Guidelines for the Management of Strabismus in Childhood
* 16 Mar 2012
* RCOphth
[Download](https://www.rcophth.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/2012-SCI-250-Guidelines-for-Management-of-Strabismus-in-Childhood-2012.pdf)
This guideline is designed for ophthalmologists managing children with strabismus (syn.squint), which is defined as a pathological misalignment of the visual axes. This is a broad subject and the reader is referred to comprehensive texts, for further information see bibliography (page 42).
The guidelines are intended to give general principles of management. It is assumed throughout this document that professionals dealing with common and uncommon cases of strabismus will have had adequate training and experience to manage children with these conditions. This document represents the current view of best practice endorsed by the College.

...

General practitioners, health visitors, paediatricians and paediatric neurologists may also become involved in the management of children with strabismus. It is desirable that these parties are committed to locally agreed care pathways, covering visual screening, referral, assessment, treatment and the monitoring of progress of children identified with strabismus.
The latter is particularly important, as it is common that information will change with development, and multiple follow up visits will be required. Written information about strabismus should be available. Adequate time should be made available by the clinicians involved, in order to explain the terminology, the possible treatments, what they involve and for the consenting procedures that are required for surgical intervention.
